name: Question 14
worked_solution:
First, we substitute $u={x}^{2}+1.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2x\,⟹\,\frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u=x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Since $u\to \infty $ when $x\to -\infty ,$ the table for the limits of integration using the rule $u={x}^{2}+1$ is as follows:

| $x$ | $-1$ | $-\infty $ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $2$ | $\infty $ |

So, the integral in terms of the new variable $u$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{-1}\frac{x}{{({x}^{2}+1)}^{3}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{\infty }^{2}\frac{1}{{u}^{3}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{2}^{\infty }\frac{1}{{u}^{3}}\,\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we proceed by setting the lower bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to -\infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{-1}\frac{x}{{({x}^{2}+1)}^{3}}\,\text{d}x & =-\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{2}^{\infty }\frac{1}{{u}^{3}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}{lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{2}^{a}{u}^{-3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}{lim}_{a\to \infty }{[-\frac{1}{2}{u}^{-2}]}_{2}^{a} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{[\frac{1}{{u}^{2}}]}_{2}^{a} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }[\frac{1}{{a}^{2}}-\frac{1}{{2}^{2}}] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }(0-\frac{1}{4}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{16}.\end{aligned}
$$
